title: Life Science Lab
subtitle: Experiments · APES Units 1, 2, 9
intro: Dr. Hale runs three live experiments: energy flow in a food web, natural selection by camouflage, and photosynthesis under different light. Pick any mission.

missions.title: Energy Flow & Trophic Cascades
missions.summary: Run a model habitat, remove the apex predators, and explain the trophic cascade using the 10% rule.

missions.title: Natural Selection: Camouflage
missions.summary: Watch birds hunt green and brown beetles on different ground, and explain how a changing environment changes a population.

missions.title: Photosynthesis & Light
missions.summary: Count oxygen bubbles from Elodea at different lamp distances, find the limiting factor, and connect it to the carbon cycle.

glossary.answer: An organism's position in a food chain: producers (plants) make food from sunlight; primary consumers (herbivores) eat producers; secondary consumers (carnivores) eat herbivores; apex predators sit at the top.

Only about 10% of the energy at one trophic level becomes new biomass at the next level. The other ~90% is used for life processes (respiration, movement) and lost as heat. That's why food chains rarely have more than 4–5 levels.

When a change at the top of a food web ripples down. Removing apex predators lets carnivores increase, which reduces herbivores, which lets plants grow back. Wolves returning to Yellowstone reduced elk browsing, and willows and aspens recovered.
Without predators to control them, herbivore populations grow and eat plants faster than the plants regrow. This can strip vegetation and lead to erosion or desertification.
An ecosystem's ability to return to balance after a disturbance. In the model, a temporary spike in herbivores returns to normal because predators and plant supply push it back.

Individuals with traits better suited to their environment survive and reproduce more, so those traits become more common over generations. The environment selects; individuals don't change on purpose.
Coloring that matches the background, making prey harder for predators to see. Beetles that match the ground are eaten less, so their color becomes more common.
A random change in DNA that can create new variations (like a different color). Mutations supply variation; natural selection then decides which variations become common.
Plants, algae and phytoplankton use light energy to turn CO2 and water into sugar, releasing oxygen: 6CO2 + 6H2O + light → C6H12O6 + 6O2.
The resource in shortest supply that controls the rate of a process. If CO2 is scarce, adding more light won't speed up photosynthesis much: CO2 is limiting.
Light intensity falls with the square of distance: twice as far gives 1/4 the light; three times as far gives 1/9.

A system that absorbs more CO2 than it releases. Forests and ocean phytoplankton remove CO2 through photosynthesis, which slows climate change. Deforestation and warmer, more acidic oceans weaken these sinks.
